Restoring the Land: A Case for Indigenous Sovereignty and the Dissolution of Federal Territorial Claims

The relationship between the United States federal government and Native American nations represents one of the longest unresolved colonial projects in modern history. From the era of westward expansion to the present day, federal authority over indigenous lands has been sustained through a combination of broken treaties, coercive legislation, and the systematic dismantling of pre-existing sovereign structures. A just future requires that the United States acknowledge the legitimacy of original indigenous title, honor its treaty obligations in their fullest sense, and restore full sovereignty and self-governance over extensive land areas to Native American nations. This is not a radical proposition; it is the logical conclusion of principles the nation has long claimed to uphold.

The Foundation of Indigenous Title

The case for indigenous sovereignty rests on a principle that requires no modern invention: the lands now claimed by the United States were, in nearly every case, the ancestral territories of complex, self-governing peoples. Before the establishment of the federal republic, Native American nations possessed their own systems of governance, economies, spiritual practices, and territorial arrangements. These were not nascent or incomplete forms of sovereignty waiting to be recognized; they were full, functioning expressions of political authority that commanded the allegiance of their members and regulated the use of land according to custom and agreement.

The Doctrine of Discovery, which the United States inherited from European colonial powers and which infamously provided that Christian European nations held title to lands inhabited by non-Christian peoples, has no legitimate basis in natural law, ethics, or—significantly—modern legal thought. Even within the framework of international law, the doctrine has fallen into comprehensive disrepute. Pope John Paul II repudiated it in 2000, and contemporary scholars of international law regard it as a relic of imperial ambition rather than a coherent principle of justice. There is no defensible reason for the United States to continue operating under a legal framework that depended entirely on the religious identity of the discoverer and the supposed inferiority of those who were already there.

The Long Record of Treaty Violations

The United States negotiated hundreds of treaties with Native American nations between 1778 and 1871. These treaties were not mere formalities; they were solemn agreements between sovereign entities, ratified by the Senate and treated as the supreme law of the land under Article VI of the Constitution. The text of these treaties often recognized specific territorial boundaries, hunting and fishing rights, and the right of self-government within those territories.

The historical record of compliance, however, is grim. Time and again, the federal government abrogated treaties when it became politically or economically convenient to do so. The Indian Removal Act of 1830, which culminated in the forced relocation of the Cherokee, Muscogee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Seminole peoples along routes that became known as the Trail of Tears, was a direct violation of treaties guaranteeing these nations the right to remain on their ancestral lands. The Dawes Act of 1887 carved up communally held tribal lands and distributed them to individual Native Americans, with the explicit purpose—stated plainly by its proponents—of extinguishing tribal landholdings. The Termination era of the 1950s sought to end the special trust relationship between the federal government and tribes altogether, with devastating consequences for the Menominee, Klamath, and many other nations.

Each of these episodes represented not a difference of policy but a violation of the binding commitments the United States had voluntarily assumed. When the federal government now claims authority over indigenous lands, it does so not on the basis of legitimate acquisition but on the basis of a long succession of broken promises, coercive statutes, and outright seizure.

Restorative Justice as a Framework

The argument for restoring indigenous sovereignty is not merely backward-looking. It draws on a forward-looking framework of restorative justice that has gained increasing influence in contemporary political thought. Restorative justice is the principle that, when one group has caused serious and ongoing harm to another, the responsible party has obligations that go beyond formal apology. These obligations include structural transformation: changing the institutional arrangements that produced the harm and creating conditions in which the affected community can determine its own future.

Native American nations have experienced not only past wrongs but the perpetuation of those wrongs in ongoing structures of dependency. The reservation system, the trust relationship, the restrictions on tribal jurisdiction—all of these continue to constrain indigenous self-determination in ways that no other community in the United States is expected to tolerate. Restorative justice requires more than compensation or symbolic recognition. It requires the restoration of the capacity for self-governance that was taken.

The Practical Case for Sovereignty

Some critics of indigenous sovereignty have argued that tribes lack the institutional capacity or resources to govern themselves. This argument has it precisely backwards. It is the federal trust system itself that has starved tribal governments of the resources, jurisdictional authority, and economic flexibility needed to thrive. Nations that have been permitted to exercise genuine self-governance—such as the Navajo Nation, the Cherokee Nation, and various Alaska Native villages—have demonstrated impressive capacity to build functioning legal systems, deliver services, and manage land sustainably.

A comprehensive restoration of sovereignty would, over time, allow Native American nations to negotiate their own economic relationships, develop their own legal codes, manage their own natural resources, and determine their own cultural and educational policies. Far from producing chaos, this would likely produce the same kind of institutional innovation that has accompanied decolonization in other parts of the world, where formerly colonized peoples have shown themselves fully capable of self-government once given the space to exercise it.

The Moral Imperative

The United States was founded on the principle that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed. Yet the government of the United States was extended to Native American lands without the consent of the peoples who lived there, and it has been sustained for centuries through a combination of force, fraud, and the constant reinterpretation of treaties and statutes to serve settler interests. There is no neutral principle of justice that can reconcile this history with the nation's founding ideals.

The dissolution of federal territorial claims and the restoration of full sovereignty to Native American nations is not a radical departure from American values. It is the fulfillment of those values, applied with consistency to the peoples whose land and labor built the country and whose continued presence reminds us of what was taken and what remains to be restored.

The work of restorative justice is not finished. It will require the United States to give up claims it has made for over two centuries and to recognize that the deepest traditions of this continent's history are not those of the republic but of the nations that long preceded it. To honor those traditions, and to live in accordance with principles of genuine justice, is to return the land.

This position draws on legal scholarship, ethical philosophy, indigenous activism, and environmental thought. Proponents—often working within the broader "Land Back" movement or associated with thinkers like Vine Deloria Jr., Walter Echo-Hawk, and Winona LaDuke—advance several interlocking arguments.

1. Historical and Legal Foundations

Original sovereignty predates the United States. Indigenous nations possessed full sovereignty over their territories long before European contact or U.S. founding. From this standpoint, the United States itself was established on land belonging to others, and any legitimate U.S. claim must derive from consent, purchase, or treaty.

Treaty obligations were systematically violated. The U.S. signed approximately 370 treaties with indigenous nations, yet the Indian Claims Commission later found that the government had broken or ignored nearly every significant one. Land cessions were often obtained through fraud, coercion, broken translations, or after the U.S. had already imposed the conditions that made "negotiation" occur.

The Doctrine of Discovery lacks legitimate grounding. The 1823 Johnson v. M'Intosh decision, which held that European "discovery" granted sovereignty over indigenous lands, has been repudiated by major religious bodies, the U.N. Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues, and an increasing number of legal scholars. The 2007 U.N. Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (which the U.S. eventually endorsed with qualifications) implicitly rejects this framework.

2. Self-Determination as a Universal Principle

The argument here parallels decolonization movements globally: that political legitimacy requires the consent of the governed and the right of peoples to determine their own political arrangements. Indigenous nations are characterized not as minority groups within a single state but as distinct peoples whose sovereignty was extinguished by force rather than relinquished by choice. Restoration is framed as completing, not initiating, decolonization.

3. Environmental and Ecological Rationale

Land management outcomes. Studies (including research published in Conservation Biology and Environmental Science & Technology) have found that indigenous-managed lands often show equal or greater biodiversity than formally protected areas, while using traditional practices like controlled burns, rotational harvesting, and watershed management.

Different relationship to land. Many indigenous worldviews conceptualize land as kin or as a sacred trust rather than as a commodity or resource. Proponents argue this orientation is increasingly relevant amid ecological crisis, offering an alternative to extractive economies.

Blocking extractive industries. Restored sovereignty would give nations the standing to refuse pipelines, mining, and other projects that have been imposed on them despite opposition, as seen in cases like Standing Rock, Oak Flat, and the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.

4. Cultural and Linguistic Survival

Place-based practices—ceremonies, plant knowledge, hunting and fishing traditions, sacred geography, oral histories tied to specific landscapes—depend on territorial integrity. Many languages and traditions are endangered precisely because of forced removal and land loss. Land return is seen as inseparable from cultural survival.

5. Economic Justice

Indigenous communities face disproportionate poverty, in significant part due to historical land theft and ongoing restrictions on land use, resource extraction, and economic development imposed by federal trusteeship. Resource extraction from tribal-adjacent or former-tribal lands has generated enormous wealth that has not flowed to original inhabitants. Full sovereignty would allow nations to capture the economic value of their territories and shape their own development paths, including opting out of extractive models.

6. Democratic and Philosophical Repair

From a standpoint emphasizing consent of the governed, ongoing occupation of land taken through violence and fraud presents a continuing injustice regardless of how much time has passed. Reparations frameworks applied to other historical injustices (slavery, internment, land dispossession in other contexts) are extended here to argue that material redress—including land—is appropriate when the original harm was material dispossession.

7. Pluralism and Federalism Extended

Proponents often point to the success of tribal sovereignty in its current limited form (tribal courts, certain governmental functions, gaming economies in some nations) as evidence that fuller sovereignty is workable. Some envision arrangements analogous to U.S. federalism, with indigenous nations coexisting as distinct polities in shared geographical space, potentially under negotiated compacts.

Important Context and Internal Debates

This position exists along a spectrum:

  • Moderate positions advocate honoring existing treaties, expanding tribal jurisdiction, returning specific sacred or culturally essential sites, and strengthening self-governance.
  • More expansive positions call for full restoration of pre-contact territories, recognition of original sovereignty as a continuing legal reality, and fundamental restructuring of U.S. political geography.
  • Indigenous critics of U.S. citizenship and federal recognition systems argue that the current "trust" relationship itself is a mechanism of control, and that full sovereignty would require ending it rather than reforming it.

The movement also encompasses significant internal indigenous debate, including questions about pan-tribal claims versus specific nations' claims, how to handle non-indigenous residents of "returned" lands, and whether restoration should be negotiated, legal, or unilateral.

The position is supported by various U.N. bodies, religious organizations, legal scholars, and an increasingly visible indigenous activist movement, while remaining contested in mainstream U.S. political discourse.

The Founding Fathers Enthusiasts Who Hate What They Founded

Perhaps the most entertaining variety of critic is the one who has read the Federalist Papers, owns a tri-corner hat for reasons they won't discuss, and can recite the Commerce Clause from memory. They will inform you at length that the Constitution is a sacred document.

It means the dissolution of state and federal claims over lands rightfully belonging to nations such as the Lakota, the Diné, the Hopi, the Haudenosaunee, the Anishinaabe, the Muscogee, the Chumash, the Shoshone, the Apache, the Crow, the Blackfeet, and the hundreds of others whose names this country has tried, for two and a half centuries, to erase.

It means the negotiation — nation to nation, as equals, not as wards and guardians — of the return of territory, water rights, mineral rights, and governance authority. It means that the children of the Diné will grow up under Diné law, that the waters of the Columbia will be governed by the treaties made with the Yakama and the Nez Perce, that the Black Hills will be what they always were: the sacred heart of a people, not a national forest carved with a president's name.

It means an end to the trust relationship as it has been misused — a leash, not a covenant — and the beginning of a true compact between free nations sharing a continent, as the Haudenosaunee themselves once imagined when they taught the newcomers their own principles of federation.

Some will say this cannot be done. I say it can be done, because every system of injustice must, eventually, face the reckoning it has postponed. Some will say it will cost too much. I say: name the price of a language extinguished, a child stolen, a treaty burned. Show me the accounting that puts a dollar on the Sacred. There is no such accounting. The debt cannot be paid. The debt can only be acknowledged — and the only acknowledgment worthy of the word is return.

Some will say this is not the America they know. I say: the America you know was built on the bones of mine. Let us build a new one — together, nation to nation, on the foundation of what should never have been disturbed: the sovereignty of the first peoples of this land.

I close with the words of Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce, who led his people across a continent in flight, and who said at the end: "I will fight no more forever." He said it not because the fight was over, but because the fight had cost him everything. Today, I ask you to take up that fight — not with weapons, but with the ballot, with your voice, with your conscience, with your relentless demand that the land remember its true owners.

The eagle does not ask permission of the ground it flies over.

The river does not ask permission of the banks that hold it.

And a people do not ask permission to return to the home that was always theirs.

Mitákuye Oyás'iŋ — we are all related. But being related does not mean being owned. It means being free, together, under the same sky, on the same ground, with justice at last.

Thank you.

Restoring Indigenous Sovereignty: A Moral Imperative for Reparative Justice

The United States’ treatment of Native American nations is a foundational injustice rooted in centuries of colonization, broken treaties, and systematic dispossession. Today, as Indigenous communities continue to resist marginalization and fight for self-determination, the time has come to address this historical wrong through transformative action. Dissolving unjust U.S. federal territorial claims and restoring extensive sovereignty to Native American nations is not merely a policy proposal—it is an ethical obligation and a step toward true restorative justice. By recognizing the inherent rights of Indigenous peoples to their ancestral lands and governance, the U.S. can begin to rectify its legacy of exploitation, honor international human rights standards, and foster equitable coexistence.

Historical Context: A Legacy of Betrayal

The dispossession of Indigenous lands is woven into the fabric of U.S. history. The Indian Removal Act of 1830, the Dawes Act of 1887, and countless forced relocations exemplify the federal government’s pattern of violating treaties and ignoring its fiduciary responsibilities. The Trail of Tears, the Wounded Knee Massacre, and the allotment policies that fragmented communal landholdings are stark reminders of a system built on theft and assimilation. These policies, justified under the guise of “civilizing” Indigenous peoples, deliberately sought to erase their cultural and political autonomy. The U.S. Constitution, while recognizing tribes as “domestic dependent nations,” was often wielded to justify paternalistic control rather than genuine partnership. This history demands acknowledgment of the deep trauma and inequality that persists today.

Indigenous Rights: Legal and Moral Foundations

Indigenous sovereignty is enshrined in international law, notably the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), which affirms tribes’ rights to self-determination, land, and cultural preservation (Articles 3, 28, 29). While the U.S. initially opposed UNDRIP, its principles align with the federal government’s own treaty obligations. Legal precedents, such as the Supreme Court’s Worcester v. Georgia (1832)—which recognized tribal sovereignty—have been ignored in practice, highlighting the gap between law and policy. Restoring land and governance to tribes would operationalize these unmet legal and moral commitments, ensuring future compliance with treaties rather than repeated betrayals.

Restorative Justice and Mutual Benefit

Returning sovereignty to Native American nations would serve as a profound act of restorative justice, addressing the intergenerational harms of colonization. Indigenous-led conservation efforts, such as the Menominee Nation’s sustainable forestry practices and the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes’ stewardship of bison, demonstrate that tribal governance can effectively protect ecosystems. Moreover, studies show that tribal-managed lands are less prone to environmental degradation compared to federal or private holdings, suggesting mutual benefits for ecological health and climate resilience. Economically, tribal autonomy offers opportunities for self-reliant development, cultural preservation, and equitable resource sharing, countering the poverty and dependency engendered by federal oversight.

Challenges and Counterarguments

Critics often question the feasibility of such a shift, citing concerns over logistics, jurisdictional conflicts, and economic impacts. However, the U.S. can draw lessons from existing tribal nations. The Navajo Nation, for instance, operates its own government, legal system, and infrastructure while engaging in cross-border trade and cooperation with states. Tribal sovereignty need not mean isolation; frameworks can be established to ensure collaboration on issues like trade, infrastructure, and environmental management. Gradual land transfers, negotiated through formal processes, could mitigate practical hurdles while honoring the principle of self-determination.

Contemporary Relevance and Ethical Imperative

The struggles of Indigenous communities remain urgent. The Standing Rock resistance against the Dakota Access Pipeline underscored ongoing marginalization, even as tribes fought for treaty-protected water rights. Legal battles over land claims, such as the Black Hills case (United States v. Sioux Nation, 1980), reveal the moral weight of compensation—tribes have rejected monetary settlements, emphasizing their desire to “have their land back.” This underscores that true justice transcends transactional fixes and requires structural change.

Furthermore, embracing Indigenous sovereignty aligns with global decolonization movements and post-colonial ethics, recognizing that marginalized peoples deserve agency over their futures. It challenges the U.S. to confront its colonial past and reimagine its identity as a nation committed to justice rather than extraction.

Conclusion: Toward a Future of Justice and Partnership

Dissolving federal territorial claims and restoring Indigenous sovereignty is a bold but necessary step toward moral reckoning. It would acknowledge historical wrongs, respect Indigenous autonomy, and foster sustainable, equitable outcomes for all. The U.S. must move beyond token gestures to implement a framework where tribal nations govern their lands with full authority. This means Congress must prioritize legislation supporting land repatriation and treaty fulfillment, while courts and leaders reaffirm Indigenous rights domestically and globally. For a nation built on Indigenous displacement, this is not only a legal duty but a chance to heal and rebuild with integrity. The path forward demands courage, but the cost of inaction—measured in continued injustice and lost wisdom—is far greater.

Restoring Sovereignty: The Case for Indigenous Land Reclamation and Self-Governance

Introduction

For centuries, the story of the United States has been told as one of progress, expansion, and democratic ideals. Yet beneath this familiar narrative lies a foundation of dispossession—the systematic theft of land from hundreds of sovereign nations that had governed this continent for millennia before European contact. The legal, moral, and historical case for dissolving federal territorial claims over Native lands and restoring genuine sovereignty to Indigenous nations is not merely compelling; it is overwhelming. This essay argues that such a restoration is not radical—it is overdue, and it is the only path consistent with justice, legal integrity, and the democratic principles the United States claims to uphold.

I. A History Written in Broken Promises

The relationship between the United States federal government and Native American nations is not one of accident or benign neglect. It is a relationship built on a staggering pattern of treaty-making and treaty-breaking that spans more than two centuries.

Between 1778 and 1871, the United States negotiated over 370 treaties with Native nations. Under the Constitution itself—Article VI, Clause 2—these treaties are designated as "the supreme Law of the Land." These were not charity documents or informal agreements. They were sovereign-to-sovereign compacts, many of which guaranteed specific land boundaries "as long as the grass grows and the waters run." The rhetorical beauty of that phrase only sharpens its betrayal.

Within years or decades of signing, nearly every one of these treaties was violated. The Cherokee removal along the Trail of Tears in 1838, the seizure of the Black Hills from the Lakota in violation of the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty, the allotment schemes under the 1887 Dawes Act that carved communal lands into individual parcels and opened "surplus" land to white settlers—all of these were acts of legal and moral fraud committed at the highest levels of American government.

The Supreme Court itself, in its own trilogy of early nineteenth-century cases—Johnson v. M'Intosh (1823), Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831), and Worcester v. Georgia (1832)—established a doctrine that simultaneously acknowledged Indigenous sovereignty while subordinating it to a "doctrine of discovery" rooted in European colonial supremacy. Chief Justice Marshall's reasoning in Johnson—that European "discovery" granted title superior to that of the people actually living on the land—was not law grounded in justice. It was the legal formalization of conquest. This doctrine remains embedded in federal Indian law to this day, most recently cited in City of Sherrill v. Oneida Indian Nation (2005). Its continued legal vitality is a stain on the American legal system.

II. The Legal and Constitutional Basis for Restoration

The argument for restoring Native sovereignty is not merely moral; it is grounded in the very legal framework the United States has established.

Treaty supremacy. The Constitution is unambiguous: treaties made under the authority of the United States are supreme law. If those treaties promised specific lands in perpetuity, then federal retention of those lands is unconstitutional on its own terms. The 1980 Supreme Court decision in United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians acknowledged that the taking of the Black Hills was a violation of the Fifth Amendment—an unconstitutional seizure of property without just compensation. The Court awarded financial compensation. The Lakota refused it. They did not want money. They wanted their land. The fact that the United States offered a check instead of land is itself a profound act of disrespect—it suggests that sovereignty can be priced, that a nation's homeland is a commodity.

The trust doctrine. The federal government has long claimed a "trust responsibility" toward Native nations—a fiduciary obligation to act in their best interest. Yet this trust relationship has functioned far more like a guardianship imposed without consent, treating sovereign nations as wards of the state. The Bureau of Indian Affairs, established in 1824, has managed Native lands, resources, and finances with a record of incompetence, mismanagement, and outright corruption so severe that the 2016 Cobell v. Salazar settlement—the largest class-action settlement in U.S. history—was required to address billions in lost revenue from mismanaged trust accounts. If a private trustee managed assets this way, they would face criminal prosecution. The federal government has never been held to equivalent account.

Self-determination as stated policy. The 1975 Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act and subsequent legislation have nominally affirmed the right of Native nations to govern themselves. But "self-determination" within a framework where the federal government retains plenary power over tribal lands, where Congress can unilaterally alter or abrogate treaties, and where tribal jurisdiction is perpetually constrained by federal and state encroachment, is self-determination in name only. Genuine self-determination requires control over territory. This is the definition affirmed by the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), which the United States endorsed in 2010, and which affirms in Article 26 that "Indigenous peoples have the right to the lands, territories and resources which they have traditionally owned, occupied or otherwise used or acquired."

III. The Moral Imperative of Restorative Justice

Justice is not served by acknowledgment alone. The United States has entered a period of increased reckoning with historical injustice—from slavery to Japanese internment—and has, in some cases, taken concrete steps toward redress. Yet the foundational injustice against Native peoples—the seizure of an entire continent—remains largely unaddressed in material terms.

Land is the center of indigenous identity. For most Native nations, land is not a commodity. It is the basis of spiritual practice, cultural continuity, language preservation, and communal identity. The forced removal of peoples from their ancestral territories was not merely an economic harm—it was an existential one, designed to sever the connection between people and place. The consequences are visible today in the epidemic rates of suicide, addiction, poverty, and health disparities on reservations—conditions that are not the result of cultural deficiency but of systematic dispossession.

The scope of the harm demands a proportional response. Consider the scale: prior to European contact, Indigenous peoples inhabited and managed virtually the entire landmass of what is now the United States—roughly 2.3 billion acres. Today, tribal land holdings amount to approximately 56 million acres, much of it held in federal trust with significant restrictions on use. This represents a reduction of roughly 97.5 percent. No serious framework of restorative justice can treat this as adequately redressed by the current arrangement.

Reparations require return, not just acknowledgment. The concept of restorative justice, as practiced in legal systems around the world, emphasizes not only acknowledgment of harm and expression of regret but the material restoration of what was taken. Financial compensation, where land cannot be returned, may be appropriate in some cases, but where the harmed party insists—as the Lakota have consistently insisted—that land itself is the remedy, justice demands that preference be honored.

IV. Addressing Counterarguments

Critics of this position will raise several objections. Each deserves serious consideration—and each ultimately fails.

"It's impractical." The claim that returning land to Indigenous governance would be logistically impossible ignores both historical precedent and the capabilities of Native nations. The Navajo Nation already governs a territory of over 27,000 square miles—larger than ten U.S. states. Many tribal governments already operate sophisticated legal, educational, and healthcare systems. Moreover, "impracticality" has never been an acceptable defense against justice. The logistics of school desegregation were complex; the logistics of emancipation were enormous. Complexity is not a moral argument.

"It would displace current residents." Restoring sovereignty does not require mass displacement. Modern frameworks can accommodate phased transitions, co-governance arrangements, leaseback agreements, and cooperative jurisdictional models—similar to arrangements between nations around the world sharing territory or governing jointly. Indigenous nations, having themselves been displaced, are unlikely to advocate for repeating that injustice upon others. The goal is governance, not ethnic cleansing—a distinction that the United States itself failed to make historically but that Native nations, having lived its consequences, would have every reason to honor.

"The United States won these lands by conquest." This is perhaps the most honest objection, and the most damning. If the legal basis for American territorial control is military conquest, then the entire American legal and moral framework—which claims to rest on consent of the governed, constitutional law, and treaty obligations—collapses into a might-makes-right philosophy incompatible with the nation's own founding ideals. The United States cannot simultaneously claim to be a nation of laws and maintain territorial claims rooted in the violation of those very laws.

V. What Restoration Could Look Like

This argument does not envision a single dramatic act of territorial transfer. It envisions a principled, phased process:

  1. Immediate recognition of all outstanding treaty claims as legally valid and enforceable, including lands guaranteed by treaties that were subsequently violated.

  2. Transfer of federal public lands within historically recognized tribal territories to Native governance, including national forests, Bureau of Land Management holdings, and military installations on former treaty lands. The federal government controls approximately 640 million acres of public land—much of it on land guaranteed to Native nations by treaty.

  3. Restoration of full sovereignty, including criminal and civil jurisdiction, natural resource management, water rights, and the authority to establish independent legal and economic systems, free from the constraints of the plenary power doctrine.

  4. Establishment of cooperative governance frameworks for transitional periods, allowing for shared infrastructure, mutual economic development, and protection of the rights of all residents.

  5. Ongoing federal financial support during the transition period, analogous to the Marshall Plan—acknowledging that nations recovering from centuries of systematic economic extraction require resources to rebuild.

VI. A Reckoning With What America Claims to Be

Ultimately, the question of Indigenous land restoration is a question about the character of the United States. If the nation genuinely believes in the rule of law, it cannot maintain territorial claims based on the systematic violation of its own treaties. If it believes in self-governance, it cannot deny that right to the peoples who governed this continent first and longest. If it believes in justice, it cannot treat 97.5 percent land dispossession as adequately remedied by poverty, restricted sovereignty, and symbolic gestures.

The philosopher John Rawls argued that justice requires us to design institutions from behind a "veil of ignorance," not knowing what position we would occupy in society. No rational person, not knowing whether they would be born Native or non-Native, would choose a system that dispossessed one group of virtually their entire homeland and then called the remainder "adequate."

Conclusion

Dissolving federal territorial claims over Native lands and restoring genuine sovereignty to Indigenous nations is not an act of charity or guilt. It is an act of legal fidelity to the Constitution's own treaty supremacy clause, an act of moral consistency with the principles of self-determination the nation professes, and an act of basic human justice for peoples who have endured centuries of systematic dispossession. The land was promised. The land was taken. The law says it should not have been. The only question that remains is whether the United States has the courage to align its actions with its own principles.

The grass still grows. The waters still run. The promises, broken though they were, still carry the weight of law. It is time to honor them.

The dissolution of U.S. federal territorial claims over Indigenous lands is not an act of charity—it is an act of justice. Recognizing and enforcing Indigenous sovereignty means acknowledging the ongoing legacy of colonialism and taking concrete steps to dismantle it. Land Back: The Moral Imperative of Restoring Native Sovereignty and Returning Stolen Lands

The United States is a nation built on stolen land.

This is not hyperbole, nor is it a radical claim. It is a historical fact. Before European colonization, hundreds of distinct Native nations—each with their own governments, cultures, and territories—thrived across the continent now called North America. The dissolution of U.S. federal territorial claims and the restoration of full sovereignty to Native nations is not a matter of political concession—it is a moral necessity, an act of restorative justice, and the only path toward reconciling this country with its foundational sins.

This is not ancient history. The oppression of Native peoples is ongoing, and the theft of their land remains an open wound. The United States cannot claim to be ajust society while it continues to occupy stolen territory and deny Indigenous nations the right to govern their own lands. It is time for land back—not as a slogan, but as a legal, ethical, and practical imperative.

I. The Historical Record: A Legacy of Theft, Violence, and Broken Promises

The dispossession of Native lands was not an accident of history. It was a deliberate, systematic campaign waged through military force, legal manipulation, and outright fraud. The scale of this theft is staggering:

  • In 1776, Native nations controlled all of what is now the continental United States.
  • By 1887, after a century of forced removals, massacres, and fraudulent treaties, Native peoples had been confined to reservations covering just 10% of their original territory.
  • Today, Native Americans hold less than 3% of their ancestral lands, much of it under federal control that restricts true sovereignty.

This was not a passive process. It was enforced through genocide and ethnic cleansing. The Trail of Tears (1838–1839) alone resulted in the deaths of 4,000 Cherokee people—nearly a quarter of the nation—as they were forcibly marched from their homelands in the Southeast to present-day Oklahoma. The Sand Creek Massacre (1864), the Wounded Knee Massacre (1890), and the Long Walk of the Navajo (1864) were not isolated incidents but part of a calculated strategy to clear land for white settlement.

Even the treaty system, supposed to be a diplomatic process between sovereign nations, was a farce. The U.S. government signed 370 treaties with Native nations—and broke every single one. The Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868, for example, guaranteed the Great Sioux Nation the Black Hills "in perpetuity." Yet, when gold was discovered in the region, the U.S. seized the land in violation of the treaty. In United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians (1980), the Supreme Court acknowledged the theft, ruling that the Black Hills were taken unlawfully and ordering compensation. The Sioux have refused the money, insisting instead on the return of their sacred land. Their stance is a testament to a simple truth: Some things cannot be bought. Some wrongs cannot be settled with cash.

The Dawes Act of 1887 accelerated land loss by breaking up tribal holdings into individual allotments, with the "surplus" land—90 million acres—sold to non-Native settlers. The Allotment Era (1887–1934) reduced Native land holdings by two-thirds. The Termination Era (1950s–1960s) sought to end federal recognition of tribes altogether, stripping them of their sovereignty and land bases.

This history is not a relic of the past. The federal trust system, supposed to protect Native lands, has been a tool of control and exploitation. The Cobell v. Salazar (1996) lawsuit revealed that the U.S. government had mismanaged and stolen billions from Native land trust accounts over more than a century. The $3.4 billion settlement in 2009 was a fraction of what was owed—and did nothing to restore the land itself.

The message is clear: The United States has never kept its word to Native peoples. It is long past time that it did.

II. The Legal and Moral Case: Indigenous Rights Are Not Negotiable

The demand for land restitution and full sovereignty is not just rooted in history—it is supported by law, both domestic and international.

A. International Law: The Right to Self-Determination

The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), adopted in 2007, explicitly affirms in Article 26: > "Indigenous peoples have the right to own, use, develop, and control the lands, territories, and resources that they possess by reason of traditional ownership or other traditional occupation or use, as well as those which they have otherwise acquired."

The U.S. endorsed UNDRIP in 2010, yet it has failed to implement its provisions. The declaration also recognizes the right to free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC)—a standard the U.S. routinely violates, from pipeline projects (e.g., Dakota Access Pipeline at Standing Rock) to mining operations on sacred lands.

Other international legal frameworks, such as International Labour Organization Convention 169 (ILO 169), also affirm Indigenous land rights. The fact that the U.S. has not ratified ILO 169 is a stain on its human rights record.

B. Domestic Law: The Hypocrisy of U.S. Jurisprudence

The U.S. legal system has long been schizophrenic on Native sovereignty. On one hand, the Constitution (Article I, Section 8) recognizes tribes as sovereign nations with which the federal government can engage in treaty-making. The Commerce Clause and "plenary power" doctrine have been used to justify federal control over Native affairs, but this control has often been paternalistic and oppressive rather than protective.

On the other hand, Supreme Court rulings have repeatedly undermined tribal sovereignty:

  • Johnson v. M’Intosh (1823) – Established the Doctrine of Discovery, a racist legal fiction that held Indigenous peoples did not hold title to their lands but merely a "right of occupancy" that could be extinguished by the federal government. This doctrine, rooted in 15th-century papal bulls, remains unoverturned to this day.
  • Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831) – Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that tribes were "domestic dependent nations" rather than fully sovereign entities, laying the groundwork for forced removal.
  • Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock (1903) – The Court ruled that Congress had "plenary power" to abrogate treaties without tribal consent, effectively giving the U.S. government unilateral authority to violate its own agreements.
  • Oliphant v. Suquamish (1978) – The Court ruled that tribes lack criminal jurisdiction over non-Native people on their own lands, a decision that has hindered tribal law enforcement to this day.

Yet, there have been important victories as well:

  • Worcester v. Georgia (1832) – Marshall ruled that tribes were sovereign nations with authority over their own lands, and that state laws had no force within tribal territory.
  • United States v. Winans (1905) – Affirmed that treaties must be interpreted as tribes would have understood them, not through a colonial lens.
  • McGirt v. Oklahoma (2020) – A landmark decision reaffirming that much of Oklahoma remains tribal reservation land, restoring jurisdiction to the Muscogee (Creek) Nation and setting a precedent for other tribes.

These rulings show that tribal sovereignty is not a gift from the U.S. government—it is an inherent right. The problem is that the U.S. has cherry-picked which aspects of sovereignty to recognize, often only when it serves its own interests.

C. The Moral Case: Justice Cannot Be Delayed Indefinitely

Beyond the legal arguments, there is a fundamental moral case for land restitution and sovereignty.

  1. Restorative Justice – If a thief steals your home, justice requires returning what was stolen, not just compensating you for its value. Land is not merely property; for Native peoples, it is sacred, ancestral, and central to identity, culture, and spirituality. No amount of money can replace the Black Hills for the Lakota, the Grand Canyon for the Hopi, or theRedwoods for the Yurok.
  2. Self-Determination – The United Nations Charter (Article 1) and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (Article 1) both affirm the right of all peoples to self-determination. The U.S. has denied this right to Native nations for centuries.
  3. Truth and Reconciliation – Other nations have confronted their colonial pasts. South Africa had its Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Canada has (imperfectly) acknowledged its residential school system as genocide. Australia has begun to recognize Indigenous land rights through Native Title. The U.S. has done none of this on a national scale. A true reckoning requires returning stolen land.

The argument is simple: If the U.S. believes in justice, it must return what was stolen.

III. The Practical Case: Why Land Restitution Benefits Everyone

Some argue that land restitution is impractical or disruptive. These objections are myopic and self-serving. The truth is that restoring Native sovereignty would benefit not just Indigenous peoples, but all Americans—and the planet.

A. Environmental Stewardship: Indigenous Land Management Works

Study after study has shown that Indigenous-managed lands have better environmental outcomes than those managed by governments or private corporations:

  • A 2019 study in Environmental Science & Policy found that Indigenous-protected areas in Canada, the U.S., and Australia had equal or higher biodiversity levels than state or privately managed lands.
  • A 2021 study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that Indigenous territories in the Amazon had significantly lower deforestation rates than non-Indigenous areas.
  • The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has recognized that Indigenous knowledge and land management practices are critical to combating climate change.

This is not a coincidence. Indigenous peoples have thousands of years of ecological knowledge, grounded in sustainable practices that prioritize long-term balance over short-term exploitation. In contrast, U.S. federal land management has often prioritized resource extraction (logging, mining, drilling) over conservation.

Examples of Indigenous Land Stewardship Success:

  • Poverty rate of 21.3% (vs. 10.5% nationally).
  • Life expectancy 5.5 years lower than the national average.
  • Suicide rates 3.5 times higher than the national average.

This is not a coincidence. Colonialism kills. Studies show that greater tribal sovereignty correlates with better outcomes in:

  • Health – Tribes with self-governance over healthcare (via the Indian Self-Determination Act) have seen reduced infant mortality and increased life expectancy.
  • Education – Tribal control over schools (e.g., Bureau of Indian Education (BIE) schools transferring to tribal management) has led to higher graduation rates and cultural preservation.

The data is clear: Native peoples do better when they control their own affairs.

IV. Rebutting the Objections: Why the Excuses Don’t Hold Up

Opponents of land restitution and full sovereignty raise several common objections. None of them are valid.

Objection 1: "It’s too late—the land is already developed or populated by non-Natives."

Australia has recognized Native Title over 40% of its land mass. New Zealand has returned land and financial settlements to the Māori. If these nations can do it, so can the U.S.
  • The alternative is perpetuating injustice. If we accept that theft is irreversible simply because time has passed, then no historical wrong can ever be righted. By that logic, slavery reparations would also be impossible. Justice delayed is justice denied—but it is still justice.

  • Colonialism has deliberately undermined tribal governance. The boarding school era, the Termination Era, and federal control over tribal lands were all designed to erode Native self-governance. Considering this history, it is remarkable how well many tribes have done—not how poorly.

Restoring Native sovereignty and returning stolen lands will not happen overnight. It will require political will, legal reforms, and a national commitment to truth and reconciliation. But it must happen. Here is a roadmap for how the U.S. can begin this process:

Step 1: Truth and Reconciliation

    • Document the full history of U.S. colonialism, including land theft, massacres, forced assimilation, and broken treaties.
    • Collect testimony from Native survivors and descendants.
    • Educate the public through school curricula, museums, and media campaigns.
  • Formally apologize for colonial crimes. While the U.S. issued a brief apology in the 2009 Native American Apology Resolution, it was buried in an unrelated defense bill and lacked any concrete actions. A real apology must be public, unqualified, and accompanied by reparations.

Step 2: Legal Reforms

  • Repudiate the Doctrine of Discovery. The U.S. must formally reject this racist legal doctrine, as Canada did in 2021.
  • Restore full tribal sovereignty. This includes:
    • Ending federal plenary power over Native lands and resources.
    • Recognizing tribal jurisdiction over all civil and criminal matters on their lands (reversing Oliphant v. Suquamish).
    • Allowing tribes to tax and regulate non-Native businesses operating on their lands.
  • Overhaul the federal trust system. The Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) and Bureau of Land Management (BLM) should be reformed or dismantled, with their land management responsibilities transferred to tribes.
  • **Pass the Land Back legislation proposed by activists and lawmakers, which would:
    • Return federal public lands to the Native nations from which they were taken.
    • Establish a process for private land restitution where feasible.
    • Provide funding and support for tribes to reacquire and manage returned lands.

Step 3: Land Restitution

  • Immediate return of sacred sites. Places like the Black Hills, Bears Ears, and the San Francisco Peaks should be immediately returned to their respective tribes, with no strings attached.
  • Return of federal lands. The U.S. government should begin returning federal lands to tribes, starting with:
    • National parks and monuments located on traditional Indigenous territories.
    • BLM lands in the West, much of which was taken from tribes without fair compensation.
    • Military bases on or near tribal lands (e.g., Fort Benning, which sits on Muscogee Creek land).
  • Compensation for private lands. Where land cannot be physically returned (e.g., in urban areas), tribes should receive fair market value compensation and preferential purchasing rights if the land becomes available.
  • Co-management as a transitional step. In areas where full restitution is not immediately feasible, co-management agreements (like those at Bears Ears) can serve as an interim measure, with the ultimate goal of full tribal control.

Step 4: Economic and Social Justice

  • Full funding for tribal programs. The federal government must honor its trust obligations by:
    • Fully funding Indian Health Service (IHS), Bureau of Indian Education (BIE), and tribal housing programs.
    • Investing in tribal infrastructure (roads, water systems, broadband).

  • Reparations for historical harms. This could include:
    • Financial compensation for stolen land, resources, and unpaid treaty obligations.
    • Restitution for cultural losses, such as languages, artifacts, and human remains held in museums and institutions (enforcing NAGPRA—Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act).
    • Education and language revitalization programs to undo the damage of boarding schools and assimilation policies.
  • Environmental justice. The U.S. must:
    • Clean up toxic waste on tribal lands (e.g., uranium mining on Navajo land, abandoned mines on Lakota land).
    • Stop permitting harmful industrial projects (e.g., pipelines, mines, and fracking operations) on tribal lands without free, prior, and informed consent.
    • Support tribal renewable energy projects to transition away from fossil fuel dependence.

Step 5: Cultural and Educational Reforms

  • Teach the true history in schools. American children should learn about:
    • The Doctrine of Discovery and its legacy.
    • The Trail of Tears, Wounded Knee, and other massacres.
    • The boarding school system and its intergenerational trauma.
    • Broken treaties and land theft.
  • Protect Indigenous languages. The U.S. should fund immersion schools, language revitalization programs, and media in Native languages.
  • Repatriate cultural artifacts and human remains. Museums and universities must return all Native artifacts, sacred objects, and human remains to their respective tribes, as required by NAGPRA but often ignored or delayed.
  • Support Indigenous media and storytelling. Funding for Native-owned newspapers, radio stations, and film projects can help preserve and share Indigenous perspectives.

VI. Conclusion: A Nation’s Moral Reckoning

The United States stands at a crossroads. It can continue to ignore its colonial past, perpetuating a system of injustice, oppression, and environmental destruction. Or it can confront its history, return what was stolen, and restore Native sovereignty.

This is not about guilt. It is not about blame. It is about justice.

Land is not just dirt and rocks. For Native peoples, land is sacred, ancestral, and alive. It is the foundation of culture, language, and identity. To deny Native nations their land is to deny their very existence as peoples.

The U.S. has a choice: It can be a nation that continues to profit from stolen land, or it can be a nation that finally does what is right.

The path forward is clear:

  1. Acknowledge the truth.
  2. Repudiate the doctrines of colonialism.
  3. Return the stolen land.
  4. Restore full sovereignty.
  5. Support Native self-determination in all its forms.

This will not be easy. There will be resistance, legal challenges, and political obstacles. But no great moral movement in history has ever been easy. The abolition of slavery, the civil rights movement, the fight for women’s suffrage—all faced immense opposition. Yet they succeeded because they were right.

Land Back is right. Native sovereignty is right. Justice is right.

The time has come. The land must be returned. The nations must be whole again.

As Lakota scholar and activist Vine Deloria Jr. once wrote: > "The more we try to be like the white man, the more we become what he has made us—reflections of his own greed and destructiveness. The only way we can survive is to be who we are, to remember our past, and to fight for our future."

The United States must let Native nations be who they are. It must remember the past. And it must fight for a future where justice prevails.

This is not a demand. It is a moral imperative. The land must be returned.

Historical Context: The Legacy of Dispossession

Dissolving U.S. territorial control would decolonize these relationships, treating Native nations as true equals rather than subjugated entities.   4. Rectifying Unjust Enrichment The wealth of the United States was built in part on the uncompensated labor and land of Indigenous peoples. Returning land to Native nations and granting them full sovereignty is believed to yield cultural, economic, environmental, and social benefits, both for Indigenous communities and for society as a whole.

Land restitution is not just about justice for the past but also about healing for the future. Benefits include:

From the perspective of Indigenous self-determination and historical justice, dissolving U.S. territorial control and returning land to Native nations is a moral, legal, and practical imperative. It is about:

  • Righting historical wrongs by addressing centuries of dispossession and oppression.
  • Honoring Indigenous sovereignty and the right to self-determination.

Restoring Justice: Returning Sovereignty and Land to Native American Nations

In the heart of the American narrative lies a profound contradiction: a nation founded on principles of liberty and justice for all built upon the theft of an entire continent from its original inhabitants. For centuries, the United States government has systematically dispossessed Native American nations of their lands, shattered their sovereignty, and broken treaty after treaty. The United States must dissolve its federal territorial claims over vast swaths of land and restore full sovereignty and independent self-governance to Native American nations. I. A Legacy of Theft and Broken Promises

The story of how the United States came to occupy North America is one of violence, deception, and betrayal. From the moment European settlers arrived, indigenous peoples were subjected to forced removals, genocidal campaigns, and the imposition of foreign laws. The doctrine of discovery and manifest destiny provided a thin veneer of legitimacy for the seizure of Native lands. Treaties, which were supposed to guarantee tribes permanent homelands and self-governance, were routinely violated whenever settlers or resources beckoned. The Trail of Tears, the Sand Creek Massacre, and the Wounded Knee massacre are but a few of the countless atrocities that marked this expansion.

By the late 19th century, the federal government had confined Native peoples to reservations—often on marginal land—and imposed a regime of forced assimilation designed to eradicate their cultures. The Dawes Act of 1887 broke up communal holdings, transferring millions of acres to white settlers. Over the next century, Native nations saw their territories shrink further through policies like termination and relocation. Today, despite limited recognition of tribal sovereignty, Native Americans remain subject to the plenary power of Congress, their lands held in trust by the federal government, and their resources exploited with little benefit to their communities. The historical record is clear: the United States acquired its territory through illegitimate means, and the original owners have never been justly compensated or restored to their rightful place.

II. The Legal and Moral Imperative for Restoration

International law and basic principles of justice demand redress for these wrongs. The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), which the United States endorsed in 2010, unequivocally affirms the right of indigenous peoples to self-determination, including the right to “freely determine their political status and freely pursue their economic, social and cultural development” (Article 3). It also calls for the restitution of lands, territories, and resources that have been taken without free, prior, and informed consent (Article 28). By endorsing UNDRIP, the U.S. has acknowledged these principles, yet it has failed to implement them in any meaningful way.

Morally, the case for restoring land and sovereignty is rooted in restorative justice—a concept that seeks to repair the harm caused by wrongdoing rather than simply punishing the perpetrator. For Native Americans, the harm includes the loss of life, culture, and land. Restitution of land is a tangible way to begin that repair. As Chief Justice John Marshall wrote in the landmark Worcester v. Georgia (1832) decision, Native nations are “distinct, independent political communities” with inherent sovereignty. That sovereignty was never lawfully extinguished; it was simply trampled by force. In 1980, the Supreme Court ruled that the taking was illegal and awarded financial compensation, but the Sioux Nation has steadfastly refused the money, demanding instead the return of their sacred land. This standoff illustrates why mere monetary compensation is insufficient; justice requires the restoration of the land itself.

Furthermore, the trust responsibility that the federal government claims over Indian lands is a relic of colonialism; true justice requires transferring control back to the tribes. This is not a matter of charity, but of right.

III. A Practical Vision for Restoring Land and Sovereignty

Some may dismiss the idea of returning vast territories as unrealistic or disruptive. Yet there are concrete, feasible pathways to achieve this goal. The key is to start with federal public lands—areas already owned and managed by the U.S. government. The federal government holds approximately 640 million acres, much of it in the western United States. These lands include national forests, grasslands, wildlife refuges, and Bureau of Land Management holdings, many of which overlap with traditional tribal territories. Transferring ownership and sovereignty over significant portions of these lands to Native nations would not require displacing private landowners. Instead, it would involve the federal government relinquishing its claim and recognizing tribal sovereignty over those areas.

We already have precedents for such transfers. In 1970, the Taos Pueblo regained control of Blue Lake and its surrounding watershed—48,000 acres of sacred land—after a decades-long struggle. In 2020, the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes took back ownership of the National Bison Range in Montana. Internationally, Canada created the territory of Nunavut in 1999, granting the Inuit self-governance over a massive Arctic region. These examples show that land restitution and the restoration of self-determination are possible through negotiation and political will.

A more ambitious plan could involve the creation of new Native-led political entities—perhaps even independent nations—on contiguous blocks of land where tribes have historical and cultural ties. This would require careful negotiation with current residents, but solutions such as buyouts, land swaps, or voluntary relocation could be implemented. The process could be phased over decades, with interim measures to build tribal capacity and ensure a smooth transition.

Tribal governments are already proving their ability to manage complex affairs. From operating successful casinos and energy enterprises to running courts and schools, many nations have demonstrated the administrative competence needed for full self-governance. Moreover, indigenous land management practices are often more sustainable and ecologically sound than those of federal agencies, offering hope for combating climate change and biodiversity loss. The Land Back movement, which has gained momentum in recent years, is not a radical fantasy but a pragmatic call for justice that aligns with both historical truth and contemporary needs.

IV. Addressing Concerns and Counterarguments

Opponents will raise several objections: that it is too late to undo history, that it would be unfair to current non-Native residents, that it would threaten U.S. territorial integrity, or that tribes are not equipped to govern large territories. These concerns, while understandable, are not insurmountable.

First, the passage of time does not erase injustice. As long as the effects of colonization persist—poverty, health disparities, cultural erosion—the moral obligation to make amends remains. Restorative justice is about repairing harm, not rewriting history.

Second, fairness to non-Native residents must be balanced with fairness to the original inhabitants. Many of these residents benefit from land that was taken unjustly; they should not be forced to leave without due process, but they also cannot claim a moral right to retain stolen property. Through negotiated settlements, fair compensation, and voluntary agreements, a just transition can be achieved. No one is advocating for a violent upheaval; we are advocating for a process that respects everyone’s dignity.

Third, the restoration of Native sovereignty need not mean the disintegration of the United States. It would mean redefining the relationship from one of domination to one of partnership. Native nations could become independent states in free association with the U.S., similar to the Compact of Free Association with Pacific island nations. Alternatively, they could remain within the U.S. political framework but with vastly enhanced self-governance, akin to the status of Puerto Rico or Washington, D.C. The exact form would be determined by the tribes themselves, in accordance with their right to self-determination.

Finally, concerns about tribal capacity are often rooted in stereotypes. Tribal governments have been managing increasingly complex responsibilities for years, often with fewer resources than state or federal counterparts. With the return of land and resources, they would have the means to invest in infrastructure, education, and healthcare, further strengthening their governance.

V. Conclusion: A Call for Courage and Justice

The United States stands at a crossroads. It can continue to perpetuate the legacy of colonization, or it can take a historic step toward justice by returning land and sovereignty to Native American nations. The latter path is not only right but also beneficial for all. It would allow Native peoples to heal and thrive, restore ecological balance, and finally align the nation’s actions with its professed ideals of freedom and equality.

The Land Back movement is growing, and public opinion is shifting. Now is the moment for elected leaders to act with courage and vision. Dissolving federal territorial claims and restoring full sovereignty—including the possibility of independence—to Native nations is a bold act of restorative justice that would redefine America’s identity and set a powerful example for the world. As Chief Seattle is often quoted, “The earth does not belong to us; we belong to the earth.” It is time to give back what was never ours to keep.

Let us embrace this opportunity to right a centuries-old wrong and build a future based on mutual respect and true self-determination. The time for justice is now.

Introduction

For over two centuries, the United States has maintained a system of federal territorial control over Native American lands, imposing a legal and political framework that undermines Indigenous sovereignty, self-determination, and cultural survival. The Historical Injustice of Federal Territorial Control

The United States was not founded on a blank slate but on the violent displacement and subjugation of Indigenous nations. From the forced removal of the Cherokee along the Trail of Tears to the systematic theft of land through broken treaties, the federal government has consistently acted as a colonial power rather than a partner in governance. The reservation system, established in the 19th century, was not a benevolent solution but a mechanism of control—confining Indigenous peoples to shrinking territories while asserting federal authority over their lives.

Even today, the federal government maintains plenary power over tribal nations, a legal doctrine derived from the 1831 Johnson v. McIntosh decision, which declared that Indigenous lands could only be acquired by the federal government, not by private entities. This doctrine has been used to justify federal interference in tribal governance, resource management, and even criminal jurisdiction—a direct violation of the principle of free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC), a cornerstone of Indigenous rights under international law.

The trust relationship between the federal government and tribal nations, while often invoked as a protective measure, is in reality a tool of ongoing dependency. Tribes remain subject to federal oversight in areas such as law enforcement, environmental regulation, and economic development, despite having their own sovereign legal systems. This contradiction—where tribes are both recognized as nations and simultaneously governed as wards of the state—must end.

The Moral and Legal Case for Full Sovereignty

1. Indigenous Peoples Are Nations, Not Domesticated Entities

The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), adopted in 2007, explicitly affirms that Indigenous peoples have the right to self-determination, including the right to freely determine their political status and freely pursue their economic, social, and cultural development (Article 3). The U.S. has signed UNDRIP but has not fully implemented it, particularly in its refusal to recognize tribal nations as fully sovereign entities outside federal control.

If the U.S. recognizes tribes as "domestic dependent nations" (a term from Worcester v. Georgia, 1832), it must ask: What does "dependent" mean? Does it mean perpetual subjugation under federal law, or does it mean a partnership of equals? The answer should be the latter. Tribal nations were sovereign before European colonization and should be sovereign again—without federal oversight unless they choose to participate in voluntary agreements.

2. Restorative Justice Requires Land Back and Political Autonomy

The theft of Indigenous lands is not ancient history—it is an ongoing process. The federal government still holds over 56 million acres of land in trust for tribes, yet it has repeatedly failed to protect these lands from exploitation, pollution, and encroachment. The Dakota Access Pipeline (DAPL) protests, the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe’s legal battles, and the ongoing fight over the Bears Ears National Monument all demonstrate that federal protection is often performative, while tribal sovereignty is systematically undermined.

True restorative justice requires:

  • The immediate return of all stolen lands where possible, with compensation for those where restitution is impossible.
  • The dissolution of federal trust relationships that allow the government to dictate tribal governance.
  • The recognition of tribal jurisdiction over all lands, including those within current reservation boundaries and any future reclaimed territories.

3. Economic and Social Liberation Through Sovereignty

Federal control has stifled Indigenous economic development. Tribes are often forced to negotiate with the federal government for basic services—healthcare, education, infrastructure—that should be self-determined. The Indian Reorganization Act (1934) and later policies attempted to modernize tribal governance, but they did so under federal supervision, limiting tribal autonomy.

If tribes were fully sovereign, they could:

  • Develop their own legal and judicial systems without federal interference.
  • Negotiate directly with corporations and foreign governments on resource extraction, trade, and investment.
  • Control their own education systems, free from federal assimilationist policies like the Boarding School Era and current BIE (Bureau of Indian Education) oversight.
  • Establish diplomatic relations with other nations, as they did before colonization.

Opponents of full tribal sovereignty often argue:

  1. "Tribes lack the infrastructure to govern independently."

    • This is a colonial mindset that assumes Indigenous peoples are incapable of self-governance. Many tribes already operate sophisticated governments, legal systems, and economies. The issue is not capability but opportunity—tribes should not be forced to beg for federal approval to exercise their rights.

  2. "Federal oversight prevents corruption and abuse."

    • Federal oversight has historically been used to suppress tribal governance, not protect it. If tribes are sovereign, they can establish their own checks and balances—just as any other nation does.

  3. "This would destabilize the U.S. legal system."

To achieve this vision, the following steps must be taken:

  2. End the federal trust relationship and return all land management authority to tribes.
  3. Recognize tribal citizenship as the sole legal status within tribal nations, with federal recognition being optional.
  4. Provide reparations for stolen lands, broken treaties, and cultural genocide.
  5. Support tribal self-determination in education, healthcare, and economic development without federal strings attached.
  6. Abolish the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) and replace it with a Tribal Sovereignty Commission that serves tribes, not the other way around.

The dissolution of federal territorial claims over Native American lands is not a radical demand—it is a restoration of what was always rightfully theirs. The United States was built on the backs of Indigenous nations, and its continued assertion of control is a violation of the most basic principles of justice. True reconciliation cannot be achieved through performative gestures like land acknowledgments or token reparations. It requires land back, sovereignty now, and the immediate dismantling of colonial structures that keep Native nations in a state of dependency.

The time for half-measures is over. Indigenous peoples deserve full self-determination, unrestricted sovereignty, and the freedom to govern their own nations—just as they did before colonization. The United States must either honor this right or admit that it remains a colonial power in all but name. The choice is clear: Justice demands sovereignty.

Title: Restoring Sovereignty: A Moral Imperative for the United States

Introduction

The United States of America, a nation built on the principles of freedom, democracy, and the pursuit of happiness, has a dark and complex history with its indigenous populations. One glaring injustice that persists to this day is the federal government's territorial claims over vast lands traditionally occupied by Native American nations. This essay strongly argues for dissolving these claims and restoring full sovereignty and independent self-governance to these lands, as a matter of indigenous rights and restorative justice.

Indigenous Rights and Self-Determination

The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), which the United States has endorsed, affirms the rights of indigenous peoples to self-determination, including the right to autonomy or self-government in matters relating to their internal and local affairs. It also recognizes their right to the lands, territories, and resources which they have traditionally owned, occupied, or otherwise used or acquired (UNDRIP, Articles 3, 26, and 27). By holding onto federal territorial claims, the United States is violating these fundamental rights of Native American nations.

Restorative Justice for Historical Wrongs

The federal government's current policy towards Native American lands is a continuation of historical injustices. The breaking of treaties, forced relocations, and assimilationist policies have led to the displacement and impoverishment of many Native American nations. Restoring sovereignty over their traditional lands is not just a matter of righting the wrongs of the past, but also a necessary step towards healing and reconciliation. It is a form of restorative justice, acknowledging the harm done and working towards reparation.

Economic and Environmental Benefits

Restoring sovereignty over traditional lands could also bring significant economic and environmental benefits. Native American nations have often been stewards of the land, practicing sustainable resource management for centuries. Returning control over these lands could lead to innovative conservation efforts and sustainable development projects that benefit both the Native American nations and the broader environment. Moreover, the economic prosperity that comes with self-governance can help alleviate the poverty and economic distress that many Native American communities face today.

Cultural Preservation and Revitalization

Traditional lands hold immense cultural significance for Native American nations. They are not just geographical locations, but the sacred spaces where their histories, spiritual practices, and identities are rooted. The United States' continued claims over these lands hinder the cultural preservation and revitalization of Native American nations. By restoring sovereignty, the federal government would be facilitating the preservation of diverse indigenous cultures, languages, and traditions.

Countering Arguments

Those against returning traditional lands to Native American nations often argue that the federal government has invested enormous resources into these lands, and that returning them would cause economic losses. However, the focus should not be on the money lost, but on the rights restored and the justice served. Moreover, the economic argument overlooks the potential benefits that could accrue if Native American nations are allowed to manage their lands responsibly and sustainably.

Conclusion

In conclusion, dissolving United States federal territorial claims and restoring full sovereignty and independent self-governance over traditional lands to Native American nations is not just a moral imperative, but a legal and historical necessity. It is a step towards rectifying historical wrongs, promoting indigenous rights, and fostering a future where Native American nations can flourish culturally, economically, and environmentally. It is time for the United States to honor its treaties, respect the rights of its indigenous peoples, and work towards a future of true coexistence and equity.
